title: The orphans' property
hookLine: give orphans their property and don't swap bad for good (4:2)

lines: A HEALTHY SHEEP FOR A SICK ONE.
cards: A father dies and leaves a flock of good sheep to his young son. An uncle will manage them, and keep the ledger, until the boy grows up. The uncle has a few sickly sheep of his own.
Nobody's checking. He could swap a healthy one for a sick one, once, quietly. Or mix the two flocks together, and let the numbers blur.
The second verse of an-Nisa sees that guardian, and that ledger, very clearly.

teach.b: Surah 4, verse 2, says: give orphans their property. Don't exchange the good for the bad. Don't eat up their wealth by mixing it with your own; that is a great sin.

Three precise warnings, aimed at exactly the tricks a guardian might use. Some commentators read these lines against Medina after Uhud, with its new orphans and widows. A few verses later, 4:6 gives a whole procedure.
Test the orphans as they near the age of marriage.

teach.h: TEST FOR SOUND JUDGMENT, THEN HAND IT OVER
teach.b: If you find sound judgment in them, rushd, hand their property over. Don't rush to spend it before they grow up. A guardian who is well off should take nothing for his work; a poor one may take what is fair.
And when you hand it over, call witnesses. Then 4:10 gives a stark picture: those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth are swallowing fire into their bellies. Why so much care?
One reason is close to home.

The Prophet ﷺ was himself an orphan. His father died before he was born, and his mother while he was still a small child. Surah 93 says to him, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?"
And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports him holding up two fingers, side by side, and saying that he and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this.
The verse turns that warmth into accounting. Love the orphan, yes, and keep the ledger straight, because theirs is theirs.

how: Muslims treat caring for orphans and guarding their wealth as a serious duty; orphan sponsorship is a widespread form of Muslim charity, and Islamic law sets rules for guardians managing a minor's property.

4:2 forbids eating up their wealth by mixing it with yours.

games.q: you're a guardian. the orphan is nearly grown. according to 4:6, when do you hand over the property?
o: only when you feel like it.
when they reach marriageable age and show sound judgment, with witnesses.
games.why: test them, and when you find rushd, sound judgment, hand it over before witnesses.

practice: Hold in mind a child who has lost a parent, someone you know, a family in your community, or children you'll never meet, without rushing to fix anything.
If you pray, you can ask God to protect them, and you might think of one real way to help: a sponsorship, a donation, time with a child who needs an adult.

wordCard.voice: Yatim, an orphan. Theirs to receive in full, with no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses, from 4:2 to 4:10. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: theirs is theirs. The Prophet knew what it was to be an orphan. Day three hundred seventy-seven, done.
